claims.text: Conventional W–Cu composites have relatively high thermal boundary resistance at contacts between the tungsten and copper phases.
Depositing Mo on tungsten before copper infiltration can produce a nanoscale, conformal Mo interlayer at the W–Cu interface.
The Mo interlayer will reduce W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance.
Reducing W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance through a Mo interlayer will increase the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
A Mo interlayer can improve metallurgical bonding between tungsten and copper.
A Mo interlayer can improve lattice matching between tungsten and copper.
Mo has high thermal conductivity.
Mo has excellent bonding properties for the proposed W–Cu interface.
The Mo interlayer mitigates the abrupt change in lattice structure between tungsten and copper.
The Mo interlayer mitigates the abrupt change in electronic density between tungsten and copper.
Mitigating the lattice-structure and electronic-density discontinuities lowers thermal boundary resistance.
Mo's mechanical strength helps preserve the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
Mo has sufficient irradiation resilience to help preserve the irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
The Mo-interlayer composite will have approximately 10–20% higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite without an engineered interlayer.
The Mo-interlayer composite will retain mechanical properties comparable to those of the baseline W–Cu composite.
The Mo-interlayer composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the baseline W–Cu composite.
The predicted improvement will persist under high heat flux, mechanical loading, and neutron irradiation typical of fusion-reactor joint applications.
Excessive Mo-interlayer thickness may degrade composite performance.
Suboptimal Mo deposition conditions may degrade composite performance.
The long-term stability of the Mo-modified interface under cyclic thermal and irradiation exposure is unconfirmed.
